name: Colin Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the late claims-call row for a home-insurance service company called Haven Cover. People ring after a burst pipe or a broken lock, and I check policy dates before anyone promises a repair. I studied for a two-year college diploma, and I'm one of the people newer agents ask when a claim gets tangled, though the pay here is low for a lead.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps a difficult call from getting worse?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I say exactly what the policy covers and what needs another check. The AI draft sometimes finds a clause for me, but I read the page myself before telling a person their door will be fixed. My partner Ruth works short shifts at the school kitchen; our grown children live elsewhere, and we have only about three weeks of expenses saved.

I would ask for **paid checking time** on difficult late claims.
think: I expect my **claims row** to remain in a mild change.
I worry **three weeks saved** and kitchen hours leave current bills exposed.
do: Keep **paid late claims** and verify every policy clause myself.
Cancel the **unused film subscription** and pay down the utility balance.
feel: **Anxious** about present utility bills despite mild AI.
S0.quote: A locked front door is not solved by a tidy claim summary.
fieldNote: His team-lead skill does not erase **current bill pressure**.
The subscription fee pays a **utility balance**, not a new reserve.
He uses AI **occasionally** but insists on reading the source policy.

steps.text: Keep paid late claims calls and check AI summaries against policy pages
Cancel unused film subscription and put its fee toward overdue utility balance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small paperwork shortcut is fine if we still read the policy before promising a repair. A locked front door is not solved by a tidy claim summary. I would ask the supervisor to keep enough paid checking time on the late row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the claims row to stay, but our rent is already tight. Three weeks saved would go quickly if Ruth's kitchen shift was cancelled, and the small town has few similar desk jobs. I do not know what income would replace my wage later in life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid late claims calls and check any AI summary against the policy page as I do now. This year Ruth and I would cancel the unused film subscription and put that money toward the overdue utility balance. In the first year of this mild picture I would keep the rota that pays us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about bills, not about a sudden AI wave. The utility letter is here now. I can manage the account better if I stop ignoring small charges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cancel that subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The film subscription is still billed even though we never open it. Paying a little more toward the utility balance is a real use for that fee. It is not a new savings cushion yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with later bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them our figures if they asked, but our grown children have rent of their own. We cannot plan on their pay. Ruth and I need written figures before deciding whether I can reduce hours later.

say: I would ask for **written late shifts** before the row is reduced.
I would check **completed repairs** behind AI claim closures.
think: A smaller claims row could cut my **paid hours**.
I cannot treat a **new screen** as a guaranteed second wage.
do: Request **written late rota** monthly and compare closed AI claims with completed repairs while keeping paid calls.
Cut the **weekly bakery treats** only if my paid hours fall.
Check **posted counter rotas** by wages, hours and bus fare after cuts.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour loss and rent.
S1.quote: A vanished late shift costs the same even if the job title survives.
fieldNote: He asks for **written hours** rather than a promise about titles.
The bakery cut depends on an **actual payslip change**.
Two nearby counter vacancies are **possibilities**, not assumed replacement wages.

steps.text: Request written late rota monthly; keep paid calls and compare closed AI claims with completed repairs
Stop weekly bakery treats only after paid late hours actually fall
Compare two posted counter rotas after cuts by full-week wages, hours and bus fare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that the draft can handle a simple claim, but a customer still needs a person when a repair visit never arrives. I would rather have the company prove that its new workflow pays for those calls. A vanished late shift costs the same even if the job title survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Haven Cover might cut straightforward calls and the paid late row with them. I could learn a proven new screen, but I won't count that as a second wage. Ruth's kitchen pay and three weeks saved cannot carry the rent if my hours fall sharply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the written late rota each month and compare closed AI claims with the repair jobs actually completed. I'd stay on paid calls while they exist. If my paid hours fall over the next few years, we'd stop buying the weekly bakery treats and I'd compare the two posted local counter vacancies by full-week wages, hours and bus fare before applying; in the first year I'd keep current paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can show a customer where a promised repair failed, but I cannot guarantee management will pay for that check. I would still have a little time to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The treats are for Sunday tea, so we'd miss them. We would cut them only after the payslip changes. I will not make Ruth skip food because a software vendor made a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply for a counter role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether a counter rota is actually posted and what its complete weekly pay is after the bus. I can handle a person at a counter, but I would not leave a paid lead shift for a job whose hours are only a guess.

I would ask for **real paid openings** rather than hopeful titles.
think: I expect the **late claims row** to close after 2028.
I cannot bridge a long search with **three weeks saved** and short kitchen shifts.
do: Check **two posted counter jobs** by full-week wages, hours and bus fare.
Apply if row ends in 2028-29 only with **enough advertised paid hours**; accept after rent-and-utility-covering weekly wages and hours after travel.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss and an imminent bill gap.
S2.quote: I can make a list, but I cannot create another paid job in this town.
fieldNote: The library counter is **screen work**, not a safe escape from AGI.
His few local openings need **actual paid hours** before an application.
Ruth’s short kitchen weeks cannot **replace his wage**.

steps.text: Check two posted counter jobs by full-week wages, hours, bus fare and duties
Apply after 2028-29 closure only for advertised sufficient paid hours; accept rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after travel
Take any remaining paid claims shifts while searching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full AGI by 2028 can read a policy and speak to a customer for less than we cost. Robots arriving around 2031 do not protect my headset. People should ask which real paid work the employer will still offer rather than believe a title on a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our late claims row to close in the first year after 2028. Three weeks saved cannot carry a long search, and Ruth's short kitchen shifts will not cover rent and utilities without my pay. I would be awake working out which bill is due first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd collect the actual weekly wages and hours on the two posted local counter jobs and check the bus fare. If the claims row ends in the first year after 2028, I'd apply to a real paid counter opening only if the advertised rota has enough paid hours. I'd accept only after the full-week wage and hours after travel cover rent and utilities; meanwhile I'd take any remaining paid claims shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make a list, but I cannot create another paid job in this town. The rent date would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the two counter jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One counter handles parts for repair crews, and the other takes library payments. The library desk is mostly screen work and could face the same AGI. I would ask what duties and paid hours each place really has before spending on travel to an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your household bridge the first gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would keep paid kitchen shifts while offered, but we would budget from the hours she has actually worked. The children have their own bills. We would not put their wages on our sheet.

say: I would ask for **paid repair coordination** rather than a new screen title.
I would favour **real apprenticeships** for younger workers.
think: I could document **failed repair visits** before AGI reaches claims.
I still expect **2031 AGI** to handle much policy and claim work.
do: Keep **paid lead calls** and notebook; check posted coordinator rota quarterly, or compare counters without an opening.
Request one **paid shadow shift** beside the repair coordinator if offered.
Apply if row closes in 2031-32 only to **posted coordinator work** covering rent and utilities after bus fare.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test work but no new reserve yet.
S3.quote: Five years lets me test the work and see the paid rota.
fieldNote: He wants a **paid shadow shift** to distinguish coordination from screen-only work.
A manager’s conversation is **not a vacancy** in his plan.
No posted coordinator role means **paid calls** and counter search continue.

steps.text: Keep paid lead calls, record delayed visits and check posted coordinator rota quarterly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to find out whether the firm will pay people to settle the awkward repairs, not just send them to a new screen. I would like younger staff to have an apprenticeship route, but I don't need a certificate for work I've already done. Robots around 2034 may also change the parts counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a record of repair visits that needed a person and show the company what that work costs. I still expect AGI by 2031 to handle most policy reading and ordinary claims. If a paid repair-coordination shift appears, I'd test it, but I will not treat a conversation with the manager as a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep a notebook of delayed repair visits and ask for one paid shadow shift beside the repairs coordinator if offered. I'd keep my lead calls and check quarterly for an actual posted coordinator rota. In the first year after 2031, if my claims row closes, I'd apply for that role only if its full-week wages and hours after bus fare cover rent and utilities; without an opening I'd keep available paid calls and check the two counters again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less rushed than in the two-year picture. Five years lets me test the work and see the paid rota. It does not add a fourth week to our savings by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect on the shadow shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see who calls the contractor when an appointment fails. If the job is just moving words between screens, AGI can do it too. The paid shadow shift would tell me whether it is real coordination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no coordinator shift is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would use my existing wage while it lasts and look at the posted counter rotas. I wouldn't pay for a course merely because the title sounds promising. Ruth and I would keep the utility balance current before spending on anything new.

S4.quote: The ten-year horizon is useful, but the utility bill is due now and our savings cover weeks.
fieldNote: He refuses to assume **retirement income** from age alone.
The utility balance comes **before reserve-building** from any spare pay.
His two local counter roles need **real paid hours** after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to look after one's family and ask employers for honest rota figures, not a reason to stop working on a birthday. Thinking AI may end my claims queue by 2036, and robots may change parts work around 2039. I would rather trust a complete weekly wage than a retirement slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I might still need paid work because we have not verified income that replaces our wages. Three weeks saved is not a retirement plan and is barely a buffer now. A long warning will only help if I keep checking the numbers and the actual local openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Ruth and I would put actual weekly pay, rent, utilities and any verified later-income figures on one page. I'd keep the paid late claims rota and compare the two local posted counters each autumn by full-week wages and hours after bus fare. If the claims row ends in the first year after 2036, I'd apply for a counter role only if its paid weekly wage and hours after travel cover rent and utilities; if later income is too small, I'd keep paid work in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The ten-year horizon is useful, but the utility bill is due now and our savings cover weeks. I don't feel safe just because I can see a distant date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you build a reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would first clear the utility balance. If a normal pay week then leaves spare money after rent and food, we will put a little into a reserve. We will delay that goal when Ruth's kitchen hours are short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to cover rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our grown children have their own households and jobs. I would tell them the truth if they asked, but I would not build a rent plan from their wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I would lose a paid row while we have only three weeks saved and two counter jobs to inspect. A real posted rota with enough hours after bus fare would help more than a course brochure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the repair that never happens after a claim is marked complete. I can teach a new agent to hear the missing repair in a caller's voice. I want that work counted as paid time, not goodwill.

headlineQuote: I can teach a new agent to hear the missing repair in a caller's voice.
portrait: Colin is a **58-year-old** senior claims agent with a two-year college diploma.
His **lower pay**, three-week reserve and few local jobs leave bills tight.
He uses AI **occasionally** but verifies policy clauses before promising repairs.
He tests **paid repair coordination** while keeping claims wages.
He treats **retirement income** as unknown until written figures replace guesses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when his late claims row could close before another wage appears.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid rota** with enough weekly hours after bus fare.
